title: Week 1 Quiz — How We Know the Past

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: Evidence created during the period being studied.
choices: primary source
bias
contextualization
historical claim
questions.explanation: Primary Source is the course term defined as: Evidence created during the period being studied.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: An interpretation produced after the period by someone analyzing evidence.
choices: contextualization
corroboration
historical claim
secondary source
questions.explanation: Secondary Source is the course term defined as: An interpretation produced after the period by someone analyzing evidence.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: Checking one source against other independent evidence.
choices: bias
corroboration
contextualization
primary source
questions.explanation: Corroboration is the course term defined as: Checking one source against other independent evidence.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: Placing evidence within the conditions, values, and events of its time.
choices: contextualization
bias
historical claim
primary source
questions.explanation: Contextualization is the course term defined as: Placing evidence within the conditions, values, and events of its time.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: A preference or perspective that can shape what a source includes or omits.
choices: bias
primary source
contextualization
historical claim
questions.explanation: Bias is the course term defined as: A preference or perspective that can shape what a source includes or omits.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the evidence and interpretation emphasized in Week 1?
choices: Every map simplifies reality and reflects choices about scale, projection, categories, and purpose.
Homo sapiens originated in Africa and migrated over many generations into diverse environments.
Historical change always follows one universal path and can be explained by a single cause.
Historical knowledge is constructed by comparing evidence rather than accepting a single account.
questions.explanation: Historical knowledge is constructed by comparing evidence rather than accepting a single account.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the evidence and interpretation emphasized in Week 1?
choices: Historical change always follows one universal path and can be explained by a single cause.
A source can be biased and still be useful when its purpose, audience, and context are examined.
Human settlement is influenced by water, climate, terrain, resources, transportation, and political boundaries.
Agriculture developed independently in several regions rather than spreading from a single universal center.
questions.explanation: A source can be biased and still be useful when its purpose, audience, and context are examined.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the evidence and interpretation emphasized in Week 1?
choices: Historical change always follows one universal path and can be explained by a single cause.
Strong historical claims identify uncertainty and explain why selected evidence is persuasive.
Food surplus supported larger settlements and specialization but also contributed to hierarchy, disease exposure, and conflict.
Migration usually results from interacting push factors, pull factors, networks, and constraints.
questions.explanation: Strong historical claims identify uncertainty and explain why selected evidence is persuasive.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest method for evaluating “Conflicting Eyewitness Accounts”?
choices: Accept the source if it was created during the period because primary sources are automatically accurate.
Compare the source with independent evidence and evaluate its origin, purpose, context, and limits.
Reject the source if it contains a point of view because useful evidence must be neutral.
Use only the most dramatic sentence because memorable details are the most reliable.
questions.explanation: Compare the source with independent evidence and evaluate its origin, purpose, context, and limits.

questions.prompt: Which response demonstrates the strongest geographic or quantitative reasoning?
choices: Ignore units and scale so attention stays on the overall appearance.
Use the visualization only if it confirms the original claim.
Assume that every mapped relationship is a direct cause.
State the observed pattern, propose an explanation, and identify what the map or data cannot prove.
questions.explanation: State the observed pattern, propose an explanation, and identify what the map or data cannot prove.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least two specific pieces of evidence, answer: How can we build a trustworthy account of the past when evidence is incomplete or disputed?
shortResponse.exemplar: A full-credit response states a defensible answer to the essential question, uses two accurate details from the week, explains how each detail supports the claim, and acknowledges one complexity or limitation.
